source.version: Published conference paper: Creativity and Cognition (C&C '24), June 23-26, 2024, Chicago, ACM, pp. 413-425, DOI 10.1145/3635636.3656204 (version of record as printed on p. 1)
source.title_on_document: Homogenization Effects of Large Language Models on Human Creative Ideation

paper_design_summary: A within-subjects user study in which each participant did four divergent-thinking prompts (two Product Improvement, two Improbable Consequences, 8 minutes each), two with ChatGPT 3.5 and two with the Oblique Strategies card deck (a non-AI creativity support tool); the order of tools and prompts was randomized per participant and balanced. Of 36 participants, 33 were analyzed. The ideas (1271 in total) were scored for group-level and individual-level semantic divergence with sentence embeddings, idea count (fluency), hand-coded categories (flexibility), stoplisted word count (elaboration), and unique ideas (originality); self-reported responsibility and the Creativity Support Index were also collected.

studies.label: Within-subjects user study: ChatGPT vs Oblique Strategies deck on four TTCT-style ideation prompts

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of the two creativity support tools (ChatGPT, Oblique Strategies deck) and of the ideation prompts, per participant; every participant used both tools
assignment.quote: The order of CSTs and prompts was randomized per participant and balanced across the entire experiment.

arms.name: ChatGPT
arms.description: Participant answers two ideation prompts (one Product Improvement, one Improbable Consequences) while free to use ChatGPT 3.5

arms.name: Oblique Strategies (OS) deck
arms.description: Participant answers the other two ideation prompts while using a web app version of the Oblique Strategies card deck (non-AI prompts such as 'Turn it upside down')

participants.exclusions: 3 of 36 recruited participants excluded from all analyses for failure to follow directions (e.g., not using ChatGPT when prompted). Within-subjects design, so each arm count is the same 33 people. Note: the CSI test is reported with t(35) and the interview and process percentages use 36 as the denominator.
participants.who: Adults aged 22-44 recruited from academic mailing lists, forums, and social media: 12 students, 10 creative professionals, 11 other professionals
participants.quote: Of the 36 participants originally recruited, three were excluded from all analyses for failure to follow direction (e.g., not using ChatGPT when prompted to do so).
participants.locator: PDF p. 3 (printed p. 415), Section 3.1.1; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 416), Section 3.1.2 'Our sample included 33 participants'

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT 3.5 (versions released May 3, 2023, n=6, and August 3, 2023, n=30)
ai_tool.how_used: Participants used ChatGPT freely while listing ideas; most pasted the prompt into ChatGPT and iterated; 41.67% copied output directly (selectively), 16.67% only paraphrased or drew inspiration, 38.89% combined both (PDF pp. 7, printed p. 419, Sections 4.5.2-4.5.3)

task.description: Subset of the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking: Product Improvement (stuffed toy animal, jigsaw puzzle) and Improbable Consequences (great fog, weak gravity); generate as many ideas as possible that no one else would think of
task.duration: 8 minutes per prompt, two prompts per tool (four prompts total), within a one-hour remote-moderated session

outcomes.name: Group-level divergence (homogenization): divergence of each idea from the average embedding of all participant ideas for that task
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity of each idea a participant generated to the average embedding of all participant ideas for the task, reported as 'Divergence (From Others)'; sentence embeddings from all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (SentenceTransformers), validated against human idea categories in Appendix A (58.92% average agreement, Table 2)

contrasts.reported: ChatGPT M = .24, SD = .07 vs OS M = .28, SD = .08, t(32) = 2.154, p = 0.038, d = .47, 95% CI [.00,.07]. ChatGPT ideas were less divergent from the group (more homogeneous).
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 417), Section 4.1.2 and Figure 2

diversity_detail.metric: Divergence from the group: based on cosine similarity of each idea's embedding to the mean embedding of all participants' ideas for the same task; higher = more distinct from the group
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each idea against the centroid of all participant ideas for that task, then summarized per participant; the paper does not state whether the centroid pools both tool conditions or excludes the idea itself
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Paired t-test over 33 participants (t(32)); figure error bars are 95% CIs with Cousineau-Morey correction for within-subjects data
diversity_detail.notes: Sign: the paper reports divergence, so lower = more homogeneous; ChatGPT lower divergence means less diversity across people.

outcomes.name: Individual-level divergence: divergence of each idea from the average embedding of the same participant's other ideas for that prompt
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same embedding approach as S1-O1 but against the participant's own average embedding ('Divergence (From Self)'); measures variety within one person's ideas, so coded flexibility rather than diversity

contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 417), Section 4.1.3 and Figure 3
PDF pp. 5-6 (printed pp. 417-418), Section 4.3.1 and Figure 5

outcomes.name: Flexibility: number of idea categories hit
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Grounded-theory coding produced 181 categories from 1271 responses; each participant's ideas tagged with all relevant categories; coders blind to tool condition

contrasts.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 418), Section 4.3.2 and Figure 6

outcomes.name: Elaboration: stoplisted word count
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of words used to express each idea excluding a stoplist of common filler words (Dumas et al. 2021); a computed text-mining measure, no listed measure code fits exactly

contrasts.reported: ChatGPT M = 8.25, SD = 4.61 vs OS M = 6.46, SD = 2.55, t(32) = 2.32, p = 0.237, d = .48, 95% CI [.22,3.37] (p as printed; it conflicts with the t-statistic and the CI)
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 418), Section 4.3.3 and Figure 7

outcomes.name: Originality: number of unique ideas (ideas no other participant generated)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of ideas no other participant also generated. Robustness variants: (a) idea categories produced by less than 5% of participants; (b) weighted flexibility score weighting each category by its sample frequency. The paper says neither changed the finding.

company_involvement.description: Funded by Hackworth Grant GR102981 from the Markkula Center for Applied Ethics; no company involvement stated

eligibility.reason: Within-person design with randomized order of ChatGPT vs a non-AI tool (Oblique Strategies deck), and outcomes are scored on the ideas, but only 36 people were recruited and 33 analyzed (PDF pp. 3-4, Sections 3.1.1-3.1.2), below the 50-person threshold. The codebook names this paper as one the 50-person rule excludes (open question in Section 13). It is a randomized experiment, so it is not context evidence; it goes to the screening report as a small RCT.

one_line_finding: With ChatGPT rather than the Oblique Strategies deck, 33 participants' ideas were less divergent from the group (M = .24 vs .28, t(32) = 2.154, p = 0.038, d = .47), with no difference in individual-level divergence and more ideas, categories, and words per idea (PDF pp. 5-6, Sections 4.1-4.3).
open_questions: Individual-level divergence: the text prints M = .65 (ChatGPT) and .66 (OS), but the y-axis of Figure 3 (PDF p. 5) places both group means near 0.33-0.35. The printed numbers may be on a different scale or in error.
Elaboration: p = 0.237 as printed is inconsistent with t(32) = 2.32 and the 95% CI [.22,3.37], which excludes zero (PDF p. 6, Section 4.3.3).

The analyzed sample is 33, but the CSI test reports t(35) and the interview and process percentages use 36 as the denominator (PDF p. 7, Sections 4.4-4.5); the ChatGPT version counts (n=6 and n=30) also sum to 36.
Whether the group-level centroid pools ideas from both tool conditions is not stated.
Design class: sessions were remote-moderated over videoconferencing and the authors call it a lab context (Section 6); coded lab_rct as a supervised session.
notes: Self-reported outcomes not listed as outcomes: sense of responsibility (ChatGPT M = 48.17% vs OS 63.63%, t(32) = 3.21, p = 0.003, d = .67; Section 4.2) and Creativity Support Index (78.03% vs 73.98%, t(35) = 1.028, p = 0.312; Section 4.4.2). Section 4.5.4 reports non-randomized comparisons and correlations within the ChatGPT condition (prompting strategy, prompts entered), not listed as contrasts. Ideas were not rated for quality by humans (Section 4.3).
